raw_response:
My reasoning, as I would think it through:

I am getting old now, 67 years, and my back hurts. My son helps sometimes but mostly it is me and my daughter-in-law working the 15 mu. So I cannot do anything too different from last year — I do what I know.

Most of my land, about 12 mu, is wheat in winter, then maize in summer. Same as everyone around here. The other 3 mu I split — a little cotton because my husband always grew some and we still have the seed dealer we trust, a small piece of peanut for our own oil, and a corner of mungbean for summer porridge. About 1.5 mu cotton, 1 mu peanut, half a mu mungbean.

For wheat, I buy one bag of compound fertilizer (50 jin) per mu before plowing, then after the wheat greens up in spring I put on urea, maybe 30 jin per mu. That is what my neighbor Old Wang does and he gets good wheat. If the price of urea is cheap I put a little more — better to waste some fertilizer than have a thin harvest. I water the wheat four times: before winter, green-up, jointing, and grain-filling. Well water is right there so why not.

For maize, I just push the seed in after wheat harvest — no plowing, no time. I use the hybrid seed the dealer gives me, same brand three years now, grows tall and ears are full. I put compound fertilizer when sowing and urea once when the maize is knee-high. Summer rain does most of the watering but I turn on the pump once or twice in July if the sky is dry. I spray for the corn borer worm, sometimes twice if I see the holes.

Cotton is trouble — many sprayings, bollworm, aphids. I spray maybe four or five times. I plow deep for cotton, that land needs it. Fertilizer similar to maize but more potash because the dealer told me cotton needs it and I saw it makes the bolls firmer.

Peanut and mungbean do not need much fertilizer — they feed themselves somehow, the old people always said so. Little bit of compound fertilizer at sowing, that is all.

I would rather spend a bit extra on fertilizer and spray than lose the harvest. A bad year we cannot eat.
